correctness.rationale: The first-derivative equations give all and only rational singular points \(P_t\); no infinity point is singular. The exact shifted Frobenius expansions cancel the linear and degree-q terms and identify the first surviving homogeneous component in each of the disjoint cases \(s<q\), \(s=q\), \(s>q\). When \(s<q\), the tangent-slope derivative has its unique critical root away from the zero locus. When \(s>q\), the cone is the product of the \(q+1\) \(\mathbb F_q\)-rational lines. At \(s=q\), direct differentiation and translation give the collision equation and the q-fold/\(q+1\)-fold root alternatives. Squarefree tangent cones imply ordinary multiple points, standard delta and rational branch counts; no such assertion is made for repeated cones. Fourteen exact modular coefficient computations check selected cases, including collision cases, but the proof is uniform and does not extrapolate from them.

originality.rationale: The originating article Theorem 1.8 specifies the rational-singularity criterion, not multiplicity or tangent-cone types. Its complete author-posted text was inspected, including the final higher-degree section and reference list. Earlier minimum-degree filling-curve theory concerns a different degree and smoothness problem. Searches for polynomial aliases, p-adic valuation, tangent splitting, singularity tables and published mathematical records did not identify this complete local trichotomy. Similar published tangent-cone results concern different geometrical objects and do not imply this family-specific formula. The existing odd-characteristic \(r=2\) local refinement is outside \(p\mid r\). Nonindexed priority risk is acknowledged.

value.rationale: The original higher-degree existence conjecture excludes the p-divisible exponent regime, making its singular local geometry a natural structural gap. Across every q and every r divisible by p, the result identifies exact multiplicity, the finite-field rational branch profile when ordinary, and a sharp valuation wall \(s=q\) with a parameter-dependent collision equation. The otherwise hidden transition from at most two rational tangents to \(q+1\) rational branches, and the existence of q-fold and \(q+1\)-fold tangent collisions, are substantial mathematical features of a published infinite family. This is not a mere numerical example, arbitrary slice, or reproduction of the original singularity-location theorem.
